claims.claim: Judaism is a monotheistic tradition whose adherents describe a covenant, a special relationship between God and the Jewish people, expressed through keeping God's laws.

BBC Religions states that Jews believe God appointed the Jewish people to be chosen in order to set an example of holiness and ethical behaviour to the world; scholars describe this idea of a chosen people as an internal theological claim, not a ranking of peoples.

The Torah is the central text of Judaism: in its narrow sense the first five books of Jewish scripture, and in a broader sense teaching, instruction, and the whole body of Jewish teaching including the oral law; tradition describes it as given to Moses.
The Tanakh is the whole of the Hebrew scriptures, an acronym of Torah (Teaching), Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings).

The Talmud is the written record of the Jewish oral law and of rabbinic discussion of it, composed of the Mishnah and the Gemara, with Jerusalem and Babylonian versions; it is the source from which the code of Jewish law (halakhah) is derived.
Mitzvot are commandments or obligations that guide Jewish practice; tradition counts 613 commandments in the Torah.
Tzedakah is charitable giving understood in Jewish tradition as a commanded duty of righteousness and justice, not optional generosity.

Tikkun olam, meaning repairing or healing the world, is a phrase that appears in rabbinic texts and that has become, in modern Jewish life, a common framing for social justice and efforts to improve society.
Shabbat, the Sabbath, is the weekly day of rest observed from Friday evening to Saturday evening, marked by candle lighting, festive meals, rest, and synagogue attendance.

Judaism includes major denominational movements — Orthodox, Conservative (also called Masorti), Reform, and Reconstructionist — with different general orientations toward revelation, Jewish law, and change; none is evaluated in this lesson.

Jewish communities are geographically and culturally diverse: Ashkenazi communities developed in Central and Eastern Europe, Sephardi communities trace their heritage to the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean world, and Mizrahi communities to the Middle East and North Africa.

Jewish lifecycle events include brit milah (ritual circumcision of boys, traditionally on the eighth day, recalling the covenant with Abraham), bar and bat mitzvah (coming of age at 13 for boys and 12 for girls in some congregations), and Jewish marriage ceremonies.
Jewish identity can be religious, cultural, or ethnic; many people identify as Jewish without observing Jewish law, and movements differ on who counts as Jewish.
An estimated 13 to 15 million Jewish people live worldwide, with the largest communities in Israel and the United States, a distribution shaped by diaspora and modern migration.

The Holocaust (Shoah), the systematic murder of about six million Jews, is commemorated in Jewish communities with memorial observances such as Yom Ha-Shoah, and scholars and community leaders describe Holocaust memory as central to modern Jewish identity and religious life.
Rabbis are Jewish spiritual leaders and interpreters of Jewish law; unlike priests in some traditions, they do not hold sacerdotal (priestly) status.

Major Jewish holidays include Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year), Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement), Passover (commemorating the exodus from Egypt), Hanukkah (the eight-day festival of lights), and Shabbat (the weekly day of rest).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who counts as Jewish is defined differently across movements.
positions: Traditional rabbinic definition: a Jew is the child of a Jewish mother (BBC Religions, beliefs page).
Some movements also accept children of Jewish fathers as Jewish (BBC Religions, beliefs page).
Movements differ on conversion requirements and on patrilineal descent.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the traditional definition and notes that movements differ, without adjudicating which definition is correct.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The meaning of the 'chosen people' idea.
positions: BBC Religions: Jews believe God appointed them as a chosen people to set an example of holiness and ethical behaviour to the world.
Reconstructionist Judaism explicitly rejects the doctrine of the Jews as God's chosen people (BBC Religions, Reconstructionist page).
Some outside observers have historically misread chosenness as a claim of superiority.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes chosenness as tradition describes it (a responsibility of example and ethical conduct), notes that not all Jews affirm the idea, and never presents it as a ranking of peoples.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The nature of the Torah's revelation.
positions: Orthodox Judaism describes the Torah as divine revelation given to Moses at Sinai (BBC Religions, Orthodox page).
Conservative Judaism describes the Torah as both divine and human: revealed by God but a human record of the encounter (BBC Religions, Conservative page).
Reform Judaism stresses that tradition must be adapted to modern life (BBC Religions, Reform page).
Reconstructionist Judaism describes the Torah as a human document, the creation of the Jewish people (BBC Religions, Reconstructionist page).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents each movement's view descriptively as the movement describes it, without ranking them.

sourceRecords.title: Bar and bat mitzvah
sourceRecords.notes: Britannica blocks automated fetch; read the Internet Archive capture of 2026-02-03 (http://web.archive.org/web/20260203025230/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bar-Mitzvah). Supports: the bar or bat mitzvah as a religious ceremony marking coming of age — 13 for boys (bar mitzvah) and, in some congregations, 12 for girls (bat mitzvah); the ceremony initiates children into religious adulthood and responsibility for upholding the commandments (mitzvot); the terms mean 'son of the commandment' and 'daughter of the commandment.' Reference only; facts synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Tikkun olam
sourceRecords.notes: Britannica blocks automated fetch; read the Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-01 (http://web.archive.org/web/20260601070613/https://www.britannica.com/topic/tikkun-olam). Supports: tikkun olam as generally translated 'healing the world'; it has had multiple interpretations over roughly two millennia; the phrase does not appear in the Hebrew Bible but first appears in rabbinic texts such as the Mishnah and Talmud; in modern ideology and Jewish conversation it indicates attempts to alleviate human suffering and spans causes including social justice, human rights, environmentalism, and more. Reference only; facts synthesized.
